answer: I would like to talk about a friend who once kept a promise to me under genuinely difficult circumstances. He is a university friend who lives in a nearby town, and we have been close for years, ever since we shared a desk in our first accounting class. A few years ago, my family moved into the flat where we live now, and it was a stressful period because my father was still busy with his business and we had very little help. My friend had promised to help me move everything on a particular weekend. As it happened, that same weekend he was offered something far more appealing, a free trip to Cox's Bazar with his colleagues, yet he turned it down without a second thought. What struck me was how [[reliable]] he proved to be, when it would have been easy to make an excuse. He showed up early, worked tirelessly all day carrying boxes and furniture up to the third floor, and never once made me feel like a burden. As for how I felt, I was touched and slightly humbled, because I knew what he had given up. I think keeping promises, especially inconvenient ones, is a real [[test of character]], and he passed it completely. His [[dependability]] deepened my trust in him enormously. Honestly, in a world where people break commitments so casually, someone who genuinely honours their word is rare and [[invaluable]]. That day taught me the kind of friend I want to be myself.

followUps.q: Do you always keep your promises?
followUps.answer: I try very hard to. If I am not sure I can do something, I would rather not promise it at all. Breaking a promise, even a small one, can [[erode]] trust surprisingly quickly.

followUps.q: Did you ever do something similar for him?
followUps.answer: Yes, last year I travelled to his town to help with his sister's wedding preparations, even though it was a busy time at work. It felt good to finally return the favour.

note: Tied the house move to my family moving into our third-floor flat (persona), named what he gave up (a Cox's Bazar trip) and added how I felt; moved plain mark 'character' to 'test of character'.
